title: Cognitive approach: schemas and models of memory
summary: How schemas shape what we encode and recall, and how the multi-store and working memory models explain memory.

keyterms.definition: A mental framework of knowledge and expectations, built from experience, that guides perception and memory.
Memory is rebuilt at recall using schemas, so it can be distorted rather than replayed exactly.
A simplified representation of a mental process, used to generate testable predictions.
Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968): memory flows from sensory memory to short-term memory to long-term memory.
A limited-capacity store holding information for a short time unless it is rehearsed.
A store of potentially unlimited capacity and duration.
Baddeley & Hitch (1974): short-term memory as an active system with several components.
The WMM component that holds and rehearses sound-based (verbal) information.
The WMM component that controls attention and coordinates the other parts.
Better recall of items at the start (primacy) and end (recency) of a list.

questions.prompt: In Bartlett (1932), English participants retold "The War of the Ghosts". What happened to the story?
options: It became longer and more detailed
It became shorter and was changed to fit their own cultural expectations
questions.explanation: Unfamiliar details were dropped or rationalised, supporting reconstructive memory shaped by schemas.

questions.prompt: Brewer and Treyens (1981) left participants in an office for about 35 seconds. Many later falsely recalled:
options: Books, which fit an office schema but were absent
questions.explanation: Schema-consistent objects were recalled even when not present, showing schemas fill gaps.

questions.statement: Bransford and Johnson (1972) found that giving a title before an ambiguous passage improved comprehension and recall.
questions.explanation: The title activated a schema (washing clothes) that helped organise the information.

questions.statement: Schema theory predicts that memory works like a video recording.
questions.explanation: Schema theory sees memory as reconstructive and prone to distortion.

questions.text: A mental framework that organises knowledge and creates expectations is a ___.
questions.explanation: Schemas allow quick processing but can lead to errors and stereotypes.

questions.text: Bartlett used serial ___, where each person retold the story to the next.
questions.explanation: In serial reproduction each retelling builds on the previous one, revealing distortions.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its finding.
questions.explanation: All four show schemas influencing cognition.

questions.prompt: A criticism of schema theory is that:
options: It is hard to observe schemas directly, so they are inferred from behaviour
questions.explanation: Schemas are hypothetical constructs; this is a measurement issue.

questions.prompt: Bartlett's procedure lacked standardization. Why does this matter?
options: It made the study more ethical
It reduced the reliability of the findings
questions.explanation: Without standard instructions or timings, results are harder to replicate.

questions.prompt: Order how a schema affects memory, according to schema theory.
items: Information is encoded in line with the schema
Recall is reconstructed and may include gaps filled by the schema
questions.explanation: Schemas influence each stage of processing.

questions.prompt: In the multi-store model, information moves from STM to LTM mainly through:
questions.explanation: Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968) proposed rehearsal transfers information to LTM.

questions.prompt: Glanzer and Cunitz (1966) found a 30-second delay before recall removed which effect?
questions.explanation: Recency depends on STM, which is lost during a delay; primacy (rehearsed items in LTM) remained.

questions.statement: HM's case supports the idea that STM and LTM are separate stores.
questions.explanation: His STM was intact but he could not transfer new information to LTM.

questions.statement: The working memory model replaced STM with a single unitary store.
questions.explanation: The WMM split STM into several components, unlike the single STM store of the MSM.

questions.text: In the working memory model, the ___ loop stores verbal information.
questions.explanation: The phonological loop holds sounds and uses subvocal rehearsal.

questions.text: Landry and Bartling (2011) found that repeating "1, 2" aloud (articulatory ___) reduced recall of letter lists.
questions.explanation: Blocking the phonological loop impaired verbal recall, supporting the WMM.

questions.prompt: Match each WMM component to its role.

pairs.right: Links information across components and LTM

questions.explanation: Baddeley added the episodic buffer in 2000.

questions.prompt: A limitation of the multi-store model is that:
options: It suggests rehearsal is the only route to LTM, but we remember many things we never rehearse
It was based only on culture
questions.explanation: Its stores are also oversimplified: STM and LTM have sub-components.

questions.prompt: Why is the central executive often criticised?
options: It is vaguely defined and hard to measure
It is identical to the phonological loop
questions.explanation: The central executive is a poorly specified construct, a measurement issue for the model.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the multi-store model.
questions.explanation: Attention moves information into STM; rehearsal moves it into LTM.
